questions.explanation: The medial cuneiform is the largest and the intermediate the smallest. The shortness of the intermediate cuneiform allows the base of the 2nd metatarsal to lock between the medial and lateral cuneiforms.

questions.stem: A construction worker who fell from a height has a heel fracture. Which associated injury must always be looked for?
questions.explanation: In a fall onto the feet the load is transmitted axially to the spine; about 10% of calcaneal fractures are accompanied by a thoracolumbar (especially L1) compression fracture, which must not be missed.

questions.stem: A 1st rib fracture is found after a road traffic accident. What should this finding suggest first?
options: High-energy trauma and injury to the subclavian artery and brachial plexus beneath it
questions.explanation: The 1st rib is short, thick and well protected, so it breaks only with high-energy trauma. Since the subclavian artery, subclavian vein and lower trunk of the brachial plexus cross it, vascular and nerve injury must be looked for.

questions.stem: Which canals connect the Haversian canals with each other and with the periosteum at right angles?
questions.explanation: Volkmann's canals run perpendicular to the long axis of the bone and connect the vessels of the Haversian canals with each other and with periosteal and endosteal vessels. Canaliculi are fine channels containing the processes of osteocytes.

questions.stem: Which is the most common type of growth plate fracture in children (Salter–Harris)?
questions.explanation: In a Salter–Harris type II fracture the line passes through the growth plate and exits through the metaphysis (Thurston–Holland fragment); it is the most common type and has a good prognosis. Type V (crush) has the worst prognosis and is often recognised late.

questions.stem: Which nerve does NOT pass through the common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn)?
questions.explanation: Through the annulus of Zinn pass the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery (optic canal), the two branches of the oculomotor nerve, the nasociliary nerve and the abducens nerve. The trochlear, frontal and lacrimal nerves pass above and outside the ring.

questions.stem: Which opening connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the nasal cavity?
questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine foramen connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the upper back part of the nasal cavity; the sphenopalatine artery and nasal nerves pass through it. The pterygomaxillary fissure opens into the infratemporal fossa.

questions.stem: Which nerves unite to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve)?
options: Deep petrosal nerve and internal carotid nerve
Lesser petrosal nerve and chorda tympani
Greater petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve
questions.explanation: The greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic fibres of VII) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic fibres from the carotid plexus) unite to form the Vidian nerve, which reaches the pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.stem: Premature closure of the sagittal suture (craniosynostosis) leads to which head shape?
questions.explanation: Growth stops perpendicular to the closed suture and increases parallel to it. In sagittal synostosis the head cannot grow sideways and lengthens front to back (scaphocephaly); it is the most common craniosynostosis. Metopic synostosis causes trigonocephaly.

questions.stem: Where does the fracture line run in a Le Fort I fracture?
options: Through the orbits, separating the face completely from the skull.
Through the neck of the mandible.
Pyramidally through the nasal root and orbital floor.
Horizontally across the maxilla just above the floor of the nose.
questions.explanation: Le Fort I separates the lower maxilla carrying the tooth sockets (floating palate). Le Fort II is a pyramidal fracture (nasal root, orbital floor), Le Fort III a craniofacial separation (through the orbits and zygomatic arches).

questions.stem: Between which vertebrae does the C5 spinal nerve exit?
questions.explanation: In the cervical region there are 8 nerves and 7 vertebrae; nerves C1–C7 exit above the vertebra of the same number and C8 exits between C7 and T1. A C5–C6 disc herniation therefore compresses the C6 root.

questions.stem: At about what age does the Y-shaped (triradiate) cartilage joining the three bones of the acetabulum ossify?
questions.explanation: The ilium, ischium and pubis are separated in the acetabulum by a Y-shaped cartilage; it ossifies at the end of puberty (15–17 years), making the hip bone a single bone.

questions.stem: Which is the narrowest anteroposterior diameter of the birth canal?
questions.explanation: The obstetric conjugate is the distance between the promontory and the nearest point on the back of the symphysis and is the narrowest anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet. On examination the diagonal conjugate is measured and 1.5–2 cm subtracted.

questions.stem: Which muscle attaches to the trochanteric fossa of the femur?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric fossa, on the inner surface of the greater trochanter, is the attachment of obturator externus. Piriformis attaches to the upper border of the greater trochanter and quadratus femoris to the quadrate tubercle.

questions.stem: What is the main reason for the high risk of avascular necrosis after fractures of the neck of the talus?
options: The growth plate of the talus stays open in adults
The talus is supplied only by the fibular artery
The talus has many muscle attachments
Blood reaches the body of the talus retrogradely from the neck
The periosteum of the talus is thick
questions.explanation: Most of the talus is covered by articular cartilage and it has no muscle attachments; blood flows to the body mainly through branches of the artery of the tarsal canal, retrogradely from the neck. A neck fracture cuts these vessels and causes necrosis of the body (Hawkins).

questions.stem: In a Bennett fracture, which muscle pulls the main (distal) fragment proximally and laterally?
questions.explanation: A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the 1st metacarpal. The small medial fragment, held by the anterior oblique ligament, stays in place; APL, attached to the base of the 1st metacarpal, pulls the main fragment proximally and laterally.

questions.stem: A motorcyclist has a pelvic ring fracture and is haemodynamically unstable. What is the most common source of bleeding in pelvic fractures?
options: Presacral and pelvic venous plexuses and fractured bone surfaces
questions.explanation: About 80–90% of bleeding in pelvic fractures comes from the venous plexuses and fractured cancellous bone; closing the ring with a pelvic binder is therefore the first step. Arterial bleeding is treated by angioembolisation.
